subdivision.heading: Joining and Separating Claims and Parties

operative_text.controlling:
3.70(1)  Two or more parties may join to bring an action, and a
plaintiff or originating applicant may make a claim against 2 or
more persons as defendants or respondents in an action, if
(a) the claim arises out of the same transaction or occurrence
or series of transactions or occurrences,
(b) a question of law or fact common to the parties is likely to
arise, or
(c) the Court permits.
(2)  This rule applies irrespective of the remedy claimed by the
plaintiff or originating applicant and whether or not 2 or more
plaintiffs or originating applicants seek the same remedy.

See also R.2.6 (representative actions) and R.2.9 (class actions). Generally speaking, the same person cannot be both plaintiff and defendant (even in

representative capacities).R.2.2(2) on overlapping partnerships is an exception. One cannot get judgment against a non-party, e.g.a mere"third party by order"under the Insurance Act. Rule 3.70 is broadly construed in the light of the severance power.Rule 3.70 is ordinarily satisfied if there is a common question of law or fact. The power to add new causes of action may

be narrower than the power to join them in the first place. Who is a party or not is very important, for it governs who has a right to notice and to make applications or participate in applications or the trial.Generally anin personamclaim can lead only to a judgment against a party, not a non-party.It is usually improper to take steps without notice to all parties, e.g.to get a "consent"order affecting a party, without telling the applications

judge or judge that that party has not consented or even got notice. The court should avoid prejudice such as lack of a chance to lead evidence or argument against the proposed judgment. The courts cannot find statutes to be unconstitutional without advance notice to the relevant Attorneys General and a chance for them to argue the point. Where the Court of Appeal had

raised the notice issue of its own motion, the decision is at least voidable, maybe even void. Defendants liable in the alternative or jointly can be joined in one suit. Usually all parties to a contract must be parties to a suit about it, unless full adjudication and justice without all parties is possible. The court cannot rectify a contract unless all the parties to

BOOK_B.title: Parties joining to bring action

commentary.text: Rule 3.70 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.70. It will be noted that in dealing with the question of misjoinder R. 36 uses the test set out in the following words, “in respect of or arising out of the same transaction or occurrence”… … a common factor of law or fact may give rise to the right to have actions joined for purposes of the proceedings. Pockar Brothers Masonry Ltd. v. Hilberta Construction Co. (1978), 6 Alta. L.R. (2d) 289 at 291 (C.A.).
